renderSubtitles.text:
Methane, ammonia and water: each is a central atom bonded to
hydrogens, and each has a different shape. Why?

Start with methane. A flat drawing puts its four
bonds in a cross, ninety degrees apart.

But every bond is a pair of electrons, and
electron pairs repel each other. In space, the
bonds can swing further apart.

They settle into a tetrahedron: one hundred nine point
five degrees between every pair of bonds.

Now ammonia. Nitrogen also has four electron
pairs, but only three are bonds. The fourth is a
lone pair, with no atom on it.

The four pairs still form a tetrahedron, but the
atoms make a pyramid. The fatter lone pair squeezes
the bonds to one hundred seven degrees.

Look from above, and the pyramid looks flat.
Only from the side does its shape show.

Water has two bonds and two lone pairs, so its atoms
are bent, and the two fat lone pairs squeeze the angle
to one hundred four point five degrees.

Tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent: the
same four electron pairs, and each lone pair
closes the angle a little more.

Electron pairs repel each other, and that
repulsion predicts the shape of a molecule.
